questions.prompt: What is the asymptotic time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements using the standard bottom-up heapify procedure?
questions.explanation: Building a heap via bottom-up heapify (starting from last non-leaf node and sifting down) runs in linear time because the work per level decreases geometrically, yielding a total of O(n).

distractor_rationales.O(n log n): This is the complexity of inserting n elements one-by-one into an initially empty heap, not bulk construction.
distractor_rationales.O(log n): This describes the cost of a single sift-down or heap operation, not the full construction.
distractor_rationales.O(n^2): This overestimates the actual work; no quadratic behavior occurs in the standard heap construction algorithm.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is most appropriate for finding the shortest path between a single source and all other vertices in a weighted, directed graph with some negative edge weights but no negative cycles?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles; it computes shortest paths from a single source in O(VE) time.

distractor_rationales.Dijkstra's algorithm: Fails with negative edge weights because it assumes greedy choice remains optimal, which is violated when negative edges exist.
distractor_rationales.Floyd-Warshall algorithm: Solves all-pairs shortest paths, not single-source — unnecessarily expensive (O(V^3)) and overkill for this requirement.
distractor_rationales.A* search: Requires a consistent heuristic and is designed for informed search in state spaces, not general weighted graphs with negatives.

questions.prompt: In an AVL tree, what is the maximum possible height difference between the left and right subtrees of any node?
questions.explanation: By definition, an AVL tree enforces that the heights of the left and right subtrees of every node differ by at most 1.

distractor_rationales.0: That would enforce perfect balance (like a complete binary tree), which AVL does not require.
distractor_rationales.2: Violates the AVL invariant; insertion or deletion would trigger rebalancing before this occurs.
distractor_rationales.log n: This is an upper bound on overall tree height, not the allowed local height difference.

questions.prompt: Which collision resolution strategy in hash tables guarantees O(1) worst-case lookup time assuming a perfect hash function and fixed table size?
questions.explanation: With two hash functions and bounded relocation, cuckoo hashing achieves O(1) worst-case successful lookup time under suitable conditions (e.g., load factor < 0.5 and good hash functions).

distractor_rationales.Separate chaining: Worst-case lookup is O(n) if all keys hash to the same bucket and degenerate into a linked list.
distractor_rationales.Linear probing: Worst-case lookup can be O(n) due to clustering, especially under high load.
distractor_rationales.Double hashing: Improves distribution over linear probing but still exhibits worst-case O(n) behavior in pathological cases.

questions.prompt: Which classic problem is NOT typically solved using dynamic programming due to absence of overlapping subproblems?
choices: Binary Search in a sorted array
questions.correct_answer: Binary Search in a sorted array
questions.explanation: Binary search has no overlapping subproblems—it partitions the problem into disjoint halves, making it naturally divide-and-conquer, not DP.

distractor_rationales.Longest Common Subsequence: Exhibits both optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems — canonical DP use case.
distractor_rationales.Matrix Chain Multiplication: Overlapping subproblems arise repeatedly when evaluating parenthesizations of subchains.
distractor_rationales.0/1 Knapsack: Subproblems (capacity, item index) recur across different recursion paths — hallmark of DP applicability.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of the 'failure function' (also called prefix function) in the KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt) string matching algorithm?
choices: To skip unnecessary character comparisons by leveraging matched prefix-suffix information
To compute the longest palindromic substring
To hash substrings for rolling comparison
To build a suffix array for the pattern
questions.correct_answer: To skip unnecessary character comparisons by leveraging matched prefix-suffix information
questions.explanation: The failure function precomputes, for each prefix of the pattern, the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix — enabling KMP to avoid backtracking in the text.

distractor_rationales.To compute the longest palindromic subst: That is solved by Manacher’s algorithm, not KMP’s failure function.
distractor_rationales.To hash substrings for rolling compariso: That describes Rabin-Karp’s use of hashing, not KMP.
distractor_rationales.To build a suffix array for the pattern: Suffix arrays are built via sorting or SA-IS algorithms — unrelated to KMP’s prefix function.

questions.prompt: In a dynamic array (e.g., Python list or Java ArrayList) that doubles in size when full, what is the amortized cost of n consecutive append operations starting from size 0?
questions.explanation: Using aggregate or accounting method, total cost of n appends is O(n) due to geometrically increasing resize costs, so amortized cost per operation is O(1).

distractor_rationales.O(log n): Misidentifies the cost of a single resize (which is O(current size)), not the amortized per-operation cost.
distractor_rationales.O(n): This is the worst-case cost of a single append during resize, not the amortized average.
distractor_rationales.O(n log n): Overestimates total cost; sum of resize costs is 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n ≈ 2n, not Θ(n log n).

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is true regarding NP-complete problems?
choices: If any NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm, then P = NP
All NP-complete problems can be solved in exponential time but never in polynomial time
NP-complete problems are a subset of P
A problem is NP-complete only if it is in NP and can be solved in O(n^k) time for some constant k
questions.correct_answer: If any NP-complete problem has a polynomial-time algorithm, then P = NP
questions.explanation: By definition, NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP; a poly-time solution to one implies poly-time solutions to all problems in NP.

distractor_rationales.All NP-complete problems can be solved i: This assumes P ≠ NP, which is unproven; the statement is conjectural, not logically necessary.
distractor_rationales.NP-complete problems are a subset of P: False — if true, then P = NP, but it's unknown and widely believed false.
distractor_rationales.A problem is NP-complete only if it is i: That describes membership in P, not NP-completeness; NP-complete problems need not be in P.

questions.prompt: What is a key advantage of using a trie (prefix tree) over a balanced BST for storing a large set of strings?
choices: Support for efficient prefix-based queries (e.g., autocomplete)
questions.correct_answer: Support for efficient prefix-based queries (e.g., autocomplete)
questions.explanation: Tries enable O(m) prefix search (where m is prefix length), independent of dataset size, making them ideal for autocomplete, spell-check, and IP routing.

distractor_rationales.Lower worst-case space complexity: Tries often use more space due to pointer overhead and sparse branching — not a key advantage.
distractor_rationales.Better cache locality during traversal: BSTs (especially B-trees) often have better locality than pointer-heavy tries; tries may suffer from poor locality.
distractor_rationales.Guaranteed O(1) insertion time: Insertion is O(m) for a string of length m — not constant.

questions.prompt: Which condition guarantees that a given edge e must be included in every minimum spanning tree of a connected, undirected, edge-weighted graph?
choices: Edge e is the unique lightest edge crossing some cut of the graph
Edge e is the heaviest edge in some cycle
Edge e connects two vertices with degree 1
Edge e has the globally minimum weight in the entire graph
questions.correct_answer: Edge e is the unique lightest edge crossing some cut of the graph
questions.explanation: The Cut Property states that the unique minimum-weight edge crossing any cut must belong to every MST.

distractor_rationales.Edge e is the heaviest edge in some cycl: By the Cycle Property, such an edge cannot belong to *any* MST — opposite of required.
distractor_rationales.Edge e connects two vertices with degree: Vertex degree says nothing about MST inclusion; irrelevant to cut or cycle properties.
distractor_rationales.Edge e has the globally minimum weight i: While often in an MST, it’s not *guaranteed* unless it crosses some cut — e.g., if it’s a self-loop or isolated, but more precisely: global minimum doesn’t imply uniqueness across *a* cut; uniqueness relative to a cut is essential.
